extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv company members, show producers and workshop teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for staging, running and monetizing live improvisation shows, and for teaching improv workshops. Covers opening/closing, tech, audience interaction, scene mechanics, touring/festivals and workshop delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting the show: opening tone and host usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Be a little wary of coming out to pumping rock music and laser displays... Slickness and showbiz is the enemy of risk and can lead to very formulaic work. But having a charismatic host who is happy to talk to the audience and welcome them to the show can be very helpful—just don’t let them dominate the whole show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-confident, high-status openings that leave little room to fail. Prefer a welcoming, charismatic host who sets a friendly mood but does not dominate. If you can afford spectacle, consider whether it reduces risk-taking and spontaneity; slickness can make work formulaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the show format quickly and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Like setting up a game, if the audience needs to understand the show’s format in order to appreciate it, then you need to explain it quickly and clearly. But there’s no point wasting time telling them things they don’t need to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give only the essential information needed for enjoyment; use the host to make the explanation funny and to give the audience practice (e.g., shouting things out). Keep setup brief to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host role and sharing hosting duties
rubrics_metrics.description: A show like Theatresports benefits from having a single dedicated host throughout, but in other formats, it may be appropriate to share the business of setting up games, keeping the show moving, sending the audience out to the bar at intermission and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether a single host is necessary for your format. Encourage many team members to interact 'as themselves' so anyone can take over hosting if needed. Don’t include a host just because it’s expected—ask what the show actually needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and sound choices for atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not you have a musician on the stage with you, you will want to have music playing in the venue when the audience enters, for atmosphere... We’ve compiled CDs with an eclectic selection of music, biased away from lyrics which can compete with the improvisers’ dialogue, but since the late 1990s have been more likely to use a laptop computer connected to the theatre’s sound system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use background music to set tone as audience arrives; bias away from lyrical tracks that clash with dialogue. Recorded music (CDs, laptop, iPod) gives stylistic breadth but reduces flexibility compared to a live musician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical support: bold lighting and sound operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Both lighting and sound operators need to be bold and fearless... This kind of coordination can’t be accomplished by technicians used to working from a cue sheet or who wait for explicit instructions before acting. The very best technicians are usually improvisers themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose technicians who can improvise and act decisively rather than only following cues. If the tech booth is constrained, ensure at least one operator is able and encouraged to make creative, on-the-fly choices. Train in-house techs and give encouragement so they grow into the role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending scenes clearly (tech and performer signals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best, most elegant and simplest way for a scene to end is for the lights to come down, ideally accompanied by a burst of music... In directed formats, it’s easy for the director to call 'scene' or wave the lights down with a gesture. Players on- and offstage can also be encouraged to give this kind of signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear, simple scene-ending mechanisms (lights down + music preferred). Allow both technicians and performers to signal scene endings (director call, stage slap, coordinated signal). If pace is sluggish, check tech contribution. Experiment with different mechanisms (time limits, Horn For Boring, buzzer) to find what suits your format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust and coordinate with your technician
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust your technician and that trust will often be rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let techs use lighting/sound resources to enhance transitions and endings; allow them creative freedom where appropriate. Ensure mutual trust so techs are empowered to respond spontaneously to the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting audience suggestions: types and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Common 'ask-fors' include: a place to be, an object, a profession, a relationship, a professional relationship... For variety, why not try to come up with new ones for each show?... “What was your grandfather’s profession?” may get you a more interesting response than 'Can someone name a profession?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary your prompts to avoid repetitive, tired answers. Use more personal or specific ask-fors to get unusual, richer material and to connect with the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling problematic or repetitive suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Another common problem is that an improviser asking for a location is hoping to hear 'cemetery' or 'library' but will more frequently hear 'Botswana.' To cope with this problem, some groups ask for 'a non-geographical location,' which is a potentially confusing phrase... One way to deal with this is to ask the person who shouted out 'Botswana' to tell you something about it which you can then use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a suggestion is geographically literal or unsuited, either elicit a usable detail from the suggester or give examples to 'knock out' overused answers. Be careful that your knock-out examples don’t drag the show into crude territory—manage audience responses without being combative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking a suggestion is a promise; repeat and thank
rubrics_metrics.description: Bear in mind that taking a suggestion makes a promise to the audience. If you take the suggestion 'doughnut' and you finish eating a doughnut before taking your dog to the vet, never mentioning doughnuts again, then the audience will feel cheated... Always repeat a suggestion once you’ve accepted it: for clarity, for volume and to reinforce your control of the stage. Also, don’t forget to thank the audience for their contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the accepted suggestion as a durable story element; incorporate it meaningfully. Repeat the accepted suggestion aloud and thank the contributor to maintain clarity and audience goodwill. Avoid 'suggestion-shopping'—don’t solicit multiple suggestions after hearing one just because you’re unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment with shows using or omitting audience suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you always get audience suggestions, try doing at least one show without them. If you never use them, see if you can incorporate them. How will you know what works if you don’t experiment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test formats with and without audience suggestions to discover what enhances your show. Use variation to keep the work fresh and to learn what engages your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using audience volunteers: respect and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Not always appropriate, but can add an extra layer of interest to many improvised shows. Be aware that rest of the audience is on the side of the volunteer you have on stage with you... You must therefore treat them with respect and kindness, make them the hero of the story, raise their status and make sure they get a round of applause for their contribution. Never get unwilling volunteers, and think twice before taking people being 'volunteered' by their friends, anyone who looks drunk or anyone you know (or what’s the point?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose volunteers carefully; never coerce participation. Protect volunteers by making them look good, elevating their status, and giving them applause. Avoid taking obvious risky volunteers (drunk, unwilling, known to you).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending the show cleanly and promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Once your show is over, get off the stage. A quick bow and a thank you and then just get the hell off. If you have other shows to promote, it’s far better to plug them right after the intermission than to let the energy of your big finish drain away as you read out a long list of your forthcoming attractions... And make sure that your technician pumps out happy music as soon as you have left the stage, or even as you are leaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close with a short bow and thank-you, then leave quickly to preserve the finale energy. Place announcements earlier in the programme (e.g., after intermission) or use fliers. Coordinate with tech to play upbeat exit music immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-show notes and feedback: structured critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you’ve had your congratulatory drink in the bar, it’s time to start thinking about the next show. Especially when starting out, some kind of notes session is advisable. This can either be a free-for-all among the cast, or (better) you can give one person who did not perform the job of scribbling down observations as the show is in progress...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold a brief, structured notes session after the show; appoint a scribe to collect observations during performance and avoid turning feedback into shouting matches. Aim to separate ego from work and keep critiques constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-specialization; broaden company skills
rubrics_metrics.description: As improvisers in one company start to find their feet, they can develop into specialists... This is a very positive thing... But as time goes on it may be a problem... As you develop as a company, while each of you will doubtless have 'favorites,' you should all be trying to broaden your skills. Have the specialists lead workshops so that each of you can acquire a bit more of that specialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cross-training so company members can cover different roles if needed. Use internal workshops led by specialists to spread skills and reduce single points of failure (e.g., if the usual scene-ender is absent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep generating variety to sustain press and audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: You may also find, if you are doing a weekly show, that press is harder and harder to come by. 'Improv Company Performs Same Show as Last Week' is hardly a gripping headline... Doing new formats with fun names, themed shows and inviting special guests to play with you can be very useful for reinvigorating the promotions business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate formats, create themed shows, invite guests, and create distinctive marketing hooks to attract press and new audiences. Produce materials (DVDs) to show promoters/exchanges the quality of your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival participation and touring expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Take your show on the road... The Edinburgh Festival has an entirely open-door policy... Improv-specific festivals tend to be smaller and friendlier. Put together a DVD so those hosting festivals can get an idea of the quality of your work... Most companies will do what they can to help you pay for your airfare... You can reasonably expect to be put up—at least in a local improviser’s spare room—and given well-attended shows to perform, often workshops to teach and always a friendly guide to the nightlife afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a good-quality DVD or promo to secure festival slots. Expect variable levels of logistical and financial support; plan travel/budget realistically. Use festivals for exposure, workshops, and cultural exchange; they can be strong bonding experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace spontaneity but balance with craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation is the only art form that can’t be edited... Improvisation’s strength—and its weakness—is its ability to reveal the unconscious mind. At best it can be daring, exciting, truthful, human and hilarious. At worst it can be self-indulgent, idiotic or pointless... A retrained brain that’s learned narrative technique and some skill in presenting stories through some understanding of status and character that’s then let off the leash is in a different league...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow unconscious inspiration and spontaneous choices onstage, but also develop narrative technique, status-awareness and storytelling skills so spontaneity yields coherent, watchable scenes. Training and craft reduce the risk of indulgent or aimless improvisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and personal material: truth without therapy
rubrics_metrics.description: Actually, the audience would love to see these things represented in stories, through characters, and would sense they were truthful without knowing they were personal... We’re not suggesting that you use improvisation as some kind of cheap therapy, rather that great playwrights and screen and TV writers—whether writing comedy or drama—are revealing their own secrets, as well as those of their friends and families, all the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal truth as raw material presented through character and story rather than direct confession. Authenticity resonates with audiences but avoid turning improv into therapy or exposing yourself unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic economics of performing improv
rubrics_metrics.description: The economics of fringe theatre are such that if you can only take fifty people per night, once you’ve paid for the theatre, the advertising and the rest of the materials for the show, most of the door money will be gone... Companies that have made real money out of improvisation... do so only after huge investment in premises and promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have realistic expectations about profitability—small houses and multi-person companies often don’t pay performers. Use shows as showcases to obtain paid gigs in TV, radio or scripted work. Consider alternative income streams (workshops, teaching) and long-term investment in premises/promotion if aiming to scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching workshops: venue, pricing, advertising and format
rubrics_metrics.description: All you need for an improv workshop is a space in which to run it and a bunch of willing students... Look around on people’s websites for local market rates and decide where to set your bar... As a general rule, we suggest that you set an upper limit on attendees—say sixteen—and then aim to break even, having paid for venue, advertising and all other expenses with half that... Advertising in listings magazines, local papers and the like are also useful and cost-effective ways to draw attention to your workshops... With the rise of the Internet, it has become easier than ever to advertise workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a suitable, affordable space (studios, community centers, church halls); research local pricing; set attendee caps (~16) and financial break-even targets (e.g., break even at ~50% attendance). Use internet/social media plus local print listings and flyers to advertise. Decide whether to run one-offs, consecutive series, or drop-in sessions based on target audience and ability-mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop class model: avoid mixed-ability drop-ins; offer progression
rubrics_metrics.description: The model has never worked for us. In the first place, it is quite hard to teach a very mixed-ability group, and the nature of a drop-in session is that there will be a constant stream of total beginners showing up. Having to teach them not to block every week will bore and frustrate the more experienced players... A possible compromise is to teach a beginner’s workshop every so often, and then run a weekly drop-in session for 'graduates' of the beginner workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer cohort-based or leveled classes to open drop-ins for mixed ability. Use a beginners’ intake followed by a graduates’ drop-in to maintain quality and retention. If running intensives (weekend Course One/Course Two), beware of logistical challenges assembling participants for follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop scheduling: weekend intensives vs weekly courses
rubrics_metrics.description: For a while, all the teaching we did was on weekends... So we ran a weekend 'Course One' for beginners, about four or five times a year, and a follow-up weekend 'Course Two' slightly less often. Course Two was always a problem, since the only people eligible for it were those who had recently taken Course One... it was hard to get a sensible number of them together at the same weekend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh pros and cons of weekend intensives (good initial immersion) against weekly classes (better continuity). If using intensives, plan for the challenge of scheduling follow-up cohorts and consider ongoing weekly options for retention.
